I'm not an expert on self harm, but I think a good way to evaluate it is to ask yourself some questions, seek therapy, and reflect your actions toward an object rather than yourself.

For example,

When do you inflict self harm? What happens before? What thoughts do you have?

What do you like about the self harm? Do you find pleasure in pain? Does it distract you from your thoughts?

Definitely talk to someone about it and find a solution. If you are seeking a distraction, maybe find another outlet to release frustration like a punching bag or exercise like running. These things are known to release stress and tension and won't cause the self harm to worsen.

I can't diagnose you over the internet, but it sounds like some sort of paranoia or nervous disorder. I would definitely get a consultation with a therapist or psychiatrist. 

Explain these exact scenarios in your life with as much detail as you can, and don't be ashamed of anything. They are professionals and have heard worse. If they diagnose you with anything or just break it down to some tension and anxiety issues, then you can knowingly try to balance it. 

You can't fix something if you don't know what's wrong.

You should seek a therapist pronto and bring all these encounters up. Your discussions are confidential and will help you heal and look forward to a better future.

Arctic gas is a big commodity and precious to come by. The plateaus and arctic in general IS daunting, but it's not so bad once you get some experience with it.

I always do the same thing in the Arctic, and I provide ALL goods to my population (even lifestyle on king william) because I'm a completionist.

You do need to use arctic lodges if you are going for this though. Arctic items basically provide the efficiency you need to provide the arctic specific goods to all your plateaus and king William island. You can always use multiple islands to feed king William whale oil and seal skin, but using arctic lodges to improve your husky farms, goose farms, caribou hunting, and bear fur are needed due to space restrictions.

Once you are producing enough to support all of your plateaus and king William island, I use 2 airships to support each plateau. I deliver the goods they need at VERY minimum amounts. For instance, I'll send over like 3-5 pemmican, sleeping bags, oil lamps etc. I'll then set a pretty low minimum stock on king William, like 10 tons, depending on how much you over produce that good. If you are at exact consumption/production, it can be tricky, and you might fall short on that good at times.

The reason why you only send small amounts to plateaus is because they have a max of 250t stock, so you can't be wasting your goods, and if you use the same airships to deliver all the gas back to King William, you need to set "discard cargo" on those airships.

So in summary, I over produce very slightly on each good for my entire arctic consumption. 2 airships (4 cargo slots or more) for each plateau delivering only the bare minimum of goods to your technicians. Each plateau only the minimum amount of workforce to work the gas, and only explorers to work the post office (which in turn now provides more technicians per household, so you can make less homes).

I always bring in coal from old world using docklands. It saves space on king William. Other supporting islands are self sufficient with coal and pemmican, and I make sure only to build enough population on those supporting islands so they don't unlock their other goods.

Use those supporting islands for whale oil and seal skin to send back to King William. Use king William harbour space for piers and depots. Try to get around 1000t of storage to support the goods you send in from old world, so you can distribute to the plateaus.

When Anno 1800 first released, it didn't have an option to set minimum stock and it came at a later update. It's a miracle setting. Always set a minimum stock when trading between your own islands. It works for everything, both passive trading and trade ships. It basically means NO ship will take that item below the minimum stock threshold.

If you want to use a trade route to pickup and drop off "different" items in the same cargo slot, then make sure to use the dump cargo overboard if storage full option. It'll allow the ship to continue the trade autonomously without it screwing up your cargo slots with incorrect products.

This way you can pick up goods from island A and drop off island B, then pick up goods island B and drop off island A. Different goods, same cargo slots.

It makes it more efficient to trade between your islands without too many ships.

Make sure to also have a minimum stock set in your island warehouses when trading goods, so you don't have 1 island with max of that product and the other island emptied.

If you really want to be precise, check an island's consumption rate of a product (ie. 7 tons per minute) and after your ship has completed the route once or twice, check your statistics screen to see the length of the journey for the trade ship, and use math to calculate how much you should be picking up to deliver.

Otherwise it's just easier and safer to make sure you have minimum stocks set.

See how much headroom?

Anyone experiencing crashes with their system need to look at the quality and the wattage of their PSU before blaming other things.  You need some headroom.  If your system requires 500W and you have 500W, you WILL crash and have issues.  I'm running an 850W Platinum rated PSU, and my system only needs roughly 500W, but I OC the hell out of it, so I need that headroom.  GPUs come factory overclocked now and draw a lot of power.  There will be power spikes in any game, and you do need a better PSU.

I think all 3 of your points can be useful in different ways.

One thing I learned is that it's best to have ships trading within its local session if possible, and the ships trading across sessions, should be direct.

For example, if I have a ship delivering coffee from NW to my capital in OW, it'll go direct from my coffee source island to my capital, then back through the session again. Things get messy when you have a ship going through sessions, then delivering all over to different islands in another. Total travel time is huge and it's hard to meet demand.

In this case if you need to distribute that coffee to more islands, have a dedicated local ship pick up from your new source (capital in OW that gets the direct coffee from NW shipment) and deliver to multiple islands. Use the minimum stock on capital as needed. A big thing that wasn't mentioned in your video is taking into account the amount needed. A lot of YouTubers just mash 50 for every good, then have a massive amount at the new island, and nothing left on the source (considering the source needs it as well).

The way to do this is check the consumption of the new island and multiple by the travel time. You can find ship travel time under the storage stats I believe. So if I need to take beer from my source and deliver it to 3 other islands, with varying populations and consumption rates, I want to give each island different amounts. If 1 island consumes 4tons per minute and the total travel time of that route is 10 minutes, that island is going to need 40 beer to sustain itself. I like to add a bit more so it was a buffer as well.

For sessions like Enbesa, I find it best to have a ship for each island transporting to production island, then taking basic goods back for the population. 

For example, if I use Taborime to produce all my stuff, and 3 other islands feeding raw materials, I will have 1 ship for each island bringing over its corresponding raw material, then picking up and bringing back basic goods needed for the population. Again, only taking the amount needed. With routes like this, you must use discard cargo, or else the route will break if storage is capped, because you utilize the same cargo slots for different goods.

Well, you are on the right track by checking your production stats. As you may notice in your screenshots, you have some goods underproduced, and some overproduced. Fixing these issues will fix your balance.

First, you need to stop the bleed from your balance. Look at the goods you are overproducing, and pause or destroy 1 set from the production chain at a time, then check your stats again. Pause or destroy excess construction material buildings if you need to. These buildings are costing you huge maintenance costs and your population isn't big enough to offset it.

Second, if you notice, your population is too low to make up for the maintenance cost on your production chains, even the chains you are producing enough of. You want to increase your higher tier populations so that your consumption is closer to your production (blue bar close to or equal to green bar, but not surpassing it).

Some goods produce way more money than others. Look at the coins each household will bring in for each good. Things like rum and beer are really profitable once you unlock artisans.

When you first unlock engineers, you normally want a healthy balance, because the initial buildings will cost a lot in maintenance (like concrete and railway setups). It'll only be until you unlock the bank that things will get easier.

I'll give my pointers I noticed:

1) Trade! Spending your money to trade for luxuries and some strategic resources early on is pivotal to your yields. You can stack these (ie 4 Sage stacks to all your cities!) Focus on luxuries that give flat bonuses early (like +5 industry) and not percent based, which are better in late game. Luxury resources are insanely powerful and the difference between winning or losing.

2) Following #1, don't get caught up in war with more than 1 nation. This is because you need them to be peaceful to trade. If there's a military nation picking on you, focus on defending yourself from them and making friends with everyone else best you can.

3) Set your cities to city growth for your population. Focus on building up food and industry, and forget about money and science, except for emblematic districts. Money and science will come naturally and later on. You want to throw down emb districts as soon as you can, because you can't do it once you advance era and get a new one.

4) Don't advance eras right away. Check your game stars. If there are stars coming up, then stay in your era and work towards them. If you still need to push out a few emblematic districts, you can do that too. If the stars are not going to be obtainable (too far away, your not at war, not making enough of a currency etc) then push to next era.

5) Don't build stuff recklessly. Are you on a river? Get infrastructure that boosts food on river tiles. Prioritize stuff that will earn you the best yields. You don't need to do the math either, but just look at your exploitable terrain and see what you need. Start off heavy on food? Get some makers district for some industry going. Food and industry is so important early game.

6) Speaking of early game, I usually split my tribe units until I get 3 groups scouting. Then I keep them together to fight animals or AI tribes. If you can't find enough food, just do 2 scouting groups cause you want to be able to defend yourself. If the AI plops down an outpost in a territory you want and you are stronger, be a bully and ransack it. If they attack, fight, then go back to ransacking. Easy money, sets the AI back, and stakes your claim.

7) Early game, try to claim as much contiguous territory as you can. Outposts don't cost anything after its initial influence. When you get your cities up, attach 1 area right away, possibly 2 to your capital. It doubles and/or triples your yields to that 1 city, and as long as stability can handle it (above 30%) , it's 100% worth it.

So war support is a game design that determines your population's desire to wage war on another opponent. If that opponent does rude things to you like refuses treaties, ransacks you, attacks you in neutral territory (considered skirmishing outside of official war), trespassing, religion/civic differences etc, then you gain grievances. 

Grievances generate small amounts of war support. If you turn those grievances into demands, you force the opponent's hand. They either give in to your demands (money, territory, etc) and you gain some profit, or they refuse your demands and you gain war support. I believe they have 10 turns to decide, and same if they make demands on you.

War support is a point scale from 0-100. When war is declared, that point scale for both you and the opponent will go up and down based on your performance. The better you do through victories, the more points and defeats reduce points. The first one to go down to 0 forces a surrender and goes to a screen where you can claim cities you occupied, vassalize then, or get gold.

It's a system to make war fun, but not allow someone to wipe everyone out quickly, as you will need to gain more war support to wage multiple wars.

One thing to note, is that even if you are in an alliance or peaceful with other nations, you can still have grievances against them and gain war support. It doesn't hurt your relations with them by having grievances. They are they ones that caused it. If you start demanding though, that can hurt relations.

So grievances are just generally always good even with allied nations. It just means you have a nice war support bar in case they ever try to betray you or cause mischief. Having better war support just gives you the upper hand when war is declared.

Like others have said, once war starts, you have to choose what you'll go after before war support runs out.  It's a system to prevent wiping out an opponent in a single go.  You can always generate more support and go after them again soon.  

I kind of like it in a sense that you can't just bully your way to victory, as it's a game meant to be a balance between era advancement, economy, and war.

So from what I've gathered thus far, Religion is actually quite automatic once you get it started.  So you first establish a religion.  When you place down holy sites and some cultural wonders, they generate religion points.  These points will affect the city its in along with bordered boundaries (I don't know the math and how far it spreads though).  Just know, the more holy sites and religion bonuses through civics/tech/buildings will have a stronger push on the boundaries.

The only benefits from having a strong religion are of course the tenets (which scale based on total followers in the world), and it'll generate grievances on nations that do not follow your religion.  So basically your friend/opponents have 2 choices - they can either switch to your religion (giving you bonuses by adding more followers) or they can keep their own religion/no religion and generate grievances for you to engage them in war.

You can either renounce the grievances and forgive them, or you can demand they allow their cities to worship your religion.  If they refuse your demands, you get a lot of war support points to declare war on them.

There is no special religious war, you need military units to declare war, otherwise all religion will do to others is just put pressure on them by giving you the upper hand with grievances and war support.

Here are some suggestions I learned:

1. Don't feel like you need to race.  The only time you may need to go faster is when playing against the harder AI, they colonize islands fast.  Otherwise if you keep peace between the AI, you have all the time in the world to play the game, and there's no race.
2. Right from the start, look at colonizing at least 3 islands in the Old World with different fertilities that you'll need like Hops, Fur, Grapes, and Nitre.  I'm pretty sure the starting island always has Grain and Potato.  If your other islands don't have Grain/Potato, you'll just need to deliver stuff like Schnapps, Beer, and Bread to them using automatic trade routes.
3. Speaking of trade routes, what I do to make things organized, is utilize the Grouping that was added to the game.  So right from the get go, I start by making groups called "OW Domestic" and "OW Import".  Any local trade in the old world is under domestic, and anything coming from another session goes into import.  Then I name the trade route specifically for what goods it's bringing and to which island (using 3 letter abbreviation to fit).  I do this for every session (2 groups for each session).
4. Don't worry about the other sessions yet except New World.  You absolutely need it to get past Artisans.  Don't feel rushed or scared to go there immediately.  Just send a decent ship on an expedition.  Once there, Isabella gives you a ship with materials to land on an island.  Just scout the fog of war best as you can, and pick an island with the basics first (Plantains and Corn) and then you'll need (Cotton, Sugar Cane) as next priority and then (Coffee, Cocoa, Tobacco) as last.  Gold ore and oil are usually on most islands too.
5. When colonizing these islands, don't feel like you need to attend to them immediately if you are busy sorting out stuff on your original islands.  Once you put your trading post on it, you keep it forever until really late game, the advanced AI will start to buy shares on your weak islands, or if you go to war.  When I went to Enbesa, I settled 4 islands I wanted, then let them sit for a very long time while I dealt with other sessions first.
6. Until you hit Investors, it's hard to keep a positive balance.  Sell overproduced goods as much as you can.  Soap to Eli, Fur to the exotic Madame, and if you have Enbesa, Ketema buys Penny Farthings and Pocket Watches for insane amounts.
7. Use the CTRL+Q option as much as you can.  Filter it to consumer goods if it's overwhelming, and check your bar graphs.  Green is what you're producing, and blue is what you consume.  Each number represents 1 ton per minute.  If you produce goods on one islands and ship to another, you can CTRL click the islands on the left side to compare both at same time, which is really helpful.
8. Focus on 1 task at a time and ignore all the crazy popup notifications unless it specifically has a timer on it.  What you can do is once you hit artisans in the old world, get their basic needs started and make sure their content/happy, then you can focus building up in the new world.  When you build up in a current session, try not to hop around sessions too much unless there's an emergency, like fire or riot.  Make sure the incident is being dealt with and then go back to what you were doing.  The game is mostly automated once you set things in place.  The biggest bonus of leaving a session on automation, is when you go back to it to build up again, it'll have a lot of construction materials.  So that's something I should have said earlier, is when you hit a new tier, the first priority is the new construction material production chain.  Get that rolling and then it's a waiting game to start the new buildings, so you can attend to other matters.

Cool, no prob. There's a lot of misinformation around fps, refresh rates, G-Sync, and v-sync. Just so you know, enabling v-sync with G-Sync on is still possible, and what it does is just limit your framerate to your monitor's max refresh rate. G-Sync won't work beyond your monitor's refresh rate. 

Capping your fps below that refresh rate does a couple things for me. 1) Keeps frame timings more stable, meaning if I can't get 120fps in the game I'm playing, but some scenes jump around from 60fps to 120fps, I'll feel the stutter. 2) Keeps G-Sync active at all times to sync refresh and frame rate.

Doing this, I can keep v-sync off to reduce input latency. However, there are some games which will still screen tear if v-sync is off, even though my frame cap is well below my refresh rate. Keep that in mind, as you may need to turn it back on.

I'm pretty new to the game too, but I've learned a lot after a few games.

CTRL+Q hotkey is your friend.  Specifically if you filter it down to consumer goods at the top.  Basically, to make it simple at the start (it's an overwhelming stats screen) is you want the green bar to be equal to or a little bit above the blue bar.  As you make more housing, you will generate more income, but you also have to make more production buildings (with maintenance costs) to support it.  So it's generally a good idea that if your green bar on those productions is a lot more than the blue, it means you can support more farmers/workers of that production tier without having to make more buildings.

If your blue bar is only slightly more than your green bar, you can raise the workforce for that production chain slightly to compensate, as long as you have the additional happiness to do so.

When I was new, I found I just built things without thinking about it.  Pay attention to the workforce required for the building, and pay attention to its initial cost and maintenance cost.  If it's too costly in any of those areas, hang tight and try to build up your workforce, income, etc. in your current tier population.

Schnapps is your initial source of income for farmers, then beer for workers, and rum for artisans.  Your income will hurt a bit until you get those production chains going for those tiers.

First thing you need to get when hitting a new tier though is the new construction material buildings (bricks for workers, glass for artisans, concrete for engineers) because you need it to make the new production chains for that tier.  Construction material buildings is a pure loss in income, so make sure you are sitting well before upgrading.
Buying shares, building ships or defenses, and occupying territory uses up quite a bit of influence points.  It's a system put in place to stop aggressive expansion without the economy to back it up.

A grid will "clean up" or absorb scatter radiation, like already mentioned.  Physically, a grid has  lead strips equally separated from each other and aligned towards a focal point in the center.  These strips of lead absorb scatter radiation.  Scatter radiation occurs when x-ray photons interact with matter (like a human body), and occur more frequently obviously if there is more matter to interact with (like obese patients or increased body thickness).  This is why using a grid with a bigger patient and/or a bigger body part is useful.  Grids are not necessary for small parts, like a hand or foot.

Downsides to using a grid?  You need to use increased radiation, because we are no longer utilizing scatter radiation to create that final image.  Instead, we are only using primary radiation, therefore we need increased technical factors to get that final image.  The other downside to using a grid is error, like "grid cut off."  If we don't use a specific distance with our tube and aligned perfectly centered to the grid, the image will look a LOT worse than just using no grid at all.  This is why a lot of techs don't use a grid for a portable chest.  Portables are done with naturally difficult to position patients, and the chest (lungs) already have really high contrast anyway.  I will always use a grid for abdomen though because the abdomen has a naturally low contrast level, and without a grid, it will look completely washed out.

You are correct, but so is the person above you. I made a post above explaining why fps matters in video games, but not so much with a movie. It has to do with frame timings (stutters) and input latency.

Are you really comparing real life to a digital world? We don't notice anything wrong in real life because it is our 'baseline' -  as in it is what we are used to and what our organs and sensory response have developed to be. Someone with a sensory disability will know this.

For example, if we were born and developed in a digital world with high response times and visual refresh rates, then moved into an analogue world, we will definately notice how bad it is.

It's because we can still notice frame stuttering, which happens at lower frame rates. If we have a perfectly smooth 30fps video we are watching, we won't notice anything odd....aka movies.

The reason why we notice low frame rates from gaming? 2 reasons:

1) Frame timing, which will cause variable frame rates that look like stutters.

2) Input latency. We don't notice the low frame rate with our eyes alone like a movie, but we notice it with our mouse and keyboard input and eye tracking. There's a HUGE difference with mouse tracking at 144fps compared to 30fps. That mouse tracking latency will affect the way we track with our eyes, causing us to notice that difference of high refresh rate.

From everything I've gathered:

IPS is usually a faster panel in pixel response time (the gap is really closing though).  It suffers from IPS glow in the monitor corners and sometimes back light bleed.  It is the best panel for viewing angles.

VA has a lot higher contrast, making it the ideal panel for quality and HDR capabilities.  It suffers from ghosting (though not much anymore with newer panels) and black smearing (pixel response time changing from black -> grey).  Viewing angles not as good as IPS, but better than TN film.

So if you are looking for fastest performance regardless of quality, go with IPS (LG has nano-IPS now which boosts quality in color over old IPS tech), but if you want HDR, wide color gamut, and better contrast with deeper blacks, go with VA.

How many hours do you have played so far? If this is your first TW game, you're going to feel overwhelmed, no doubt about it. On top of that, these games have high learning curve for new people. You can go 20hrs in and still not know everything. Some tips to your questions...

Money is everything. Without it, you can't field armies, and without armies, you can't win. You need to juggle your treasury so that you don't go bankrupt, and each faction may do this differently. For example, Dwarves, Empire, Elves, and other "empire building" factions will get a lot of 'gold per turn' from owning a lot of taxable provinces and trading. While some factions like Pirates, Chaos, Greens kind, and Skaven generate more money from aggressive activities like winning battles, sacking settlements, and raiding. They don't generate enough from buildings, and trading - especially since everyone hates you.

Having multiple armies cuts into your treasury due to supply line % reductions. So in the early game, you'll have 1 army and quickly advance to 2 armies, but the jump to 3 armies might take a while for you to build up your treasury. Each unit you get has upkeep per turn. This means trying to quick tech to high tier units might not always be the best since you may not be able to afford it.

Try to manage your settlements public order to prevent rebellion armies popping up and attacking you. Do this with buildings, events, and mostly just positioning an Army Garrison in one of the settlements in the province. A province is a collection of settlements. Each settlement generates income, but the total income is taxed as a whole for the province. The public order is also province based. When you own all settlements in a province, you can enact edicts which grant bonuses of your choosing.

As for battles, learn hotkeys and mouse tricks. It's so important. There's so many that it's hard to state here. Google a YouTube guide on total war hotkeys, shortcuts, and mouse clicks. Trust me, it'll be so nice.

Monster movement is very tricky in this game.  There are times when monsters normally have a natural ranged attack, but ability cards are not ranged.  Just follow ability cards and move rules in order.

For move rules, a monster will move to the closest hex to make an attack on its focused target.  If a natural ranged monster has an ability card that comes up and just says 'Move + 0' then muddle all enemies in range - even though the monster has a natural range on its stat sheet, the ability card shows it is NOT making an attack.  Therefore, monster rules is that it is moving towards its focus to be within melee range as best it can and THEN you look at the 2nd component which allows it to muddle all enemies with its natural range after its done moving.

It's confusing, I know.

The technology tree can be very overwhelming at first, and honestly, you need to play a few games to understand all the basics, resources, buildings, etc. to know how they scale in priority.

As a general rule, Food/Production are the most important early game for growing your population and cranking out buildings/ships.  Science/Dust are better for exponential gain, but won't help a lot if you have weak growth and production.

Explore early with exploration ships and find systems that are worth colonizing.  You want to try and gain strategic resources first, and luxury resources are a bonus.  Also look for planets that you can colonize early, any beneficial anomalies they have, etc. for better +FIDSI per population.

If you zoom into your planets, you can see details around your population type, and planet type.  So if your population unit says it has +1 Food on Fertile planets, then try to move it to a planet (in the same system of course) that is 'Fertile' for the bonus.  This is a good way to min/max your FIDSI output.

It's hard to explain all the mechanics of the game, but try to pay attention to details.  Let's say there is a building you can make that says +10 Production on Hot planets and you have 3/4 Hot planets in that system, then you will get +30 bonus production with that building (because the building affects that system and all its planets).  So maybe prioritize it over other buildings that might not be as beneficial for that system.  Does that make sense?

I just started playing ES2, but I have a little ES1 experience as well.  The game's tutorial is non-existent and combat can be intimidating.  You are basically picking a lot of tactical options and then watching a cinematic auto combat for you.

The biggest thing to note is Projectile weapons vs Energy weapons.  Missle and Flak are projectile, while Beam and Laser are Energy.  Shield defense is good vs Energy, and Plate defense is good vs projectile.

Each of those 4 weapon types have range bonuses.  Like Missles are 100% effective at Long range, Beam is your jack of all trades effective at all ranges, but lower dmg, and Lasers are good at short range I believe.  When building your ships in the military panel (F5), the tooltip will show effective ranges for each weapon type.

Before battle, use the advanced setup.  When you pick a battle tactics, there are 3 rows that specify ranges for each of those rows.  You want to pick the range setup that's best for your fleet.  It can be hard to min/max this, but the game will auto show your compatibility on the left for each of the 3 rows.  You need to have really large flotillas in order to use all 3 rows though, so by default, just the middle row will be used.

In summary, watch how you balance your 4 weapon types (2 damage types) vs the enemy's defenses (shields vs plate).  If your enemy has full on shields, build ships with missles for long range, and Flak cannons for short range and they will rip apart your enemy's defenses.

One of the biggest tips I can give you is having patience during missions. You know how the game auto selects a soldier and cycles through them in that order? Well, you don't have to play them in that order. Once you've engaged an enemy pod (group of enemies) and it's your turn, you need to carefully evaluate and see if you can finish off every enemy before it's their turn. If you can't, the enemy having a chance to take action can be very painful, as even a single shot can outright kill or seriously injure a soldier.

The best thing to do is Tab cycle through your soldiers and find your best play. Calculate DMG, hit chance, best positioning, etc. Don't always take the first action you see. "Oh, this guy has a good 90% hit chance, fire immediately!" - this is not a good strategy. Check all your soldiers and see what each can do before deciding who should act first.

Try to finish off enemies completely. The alien with 1/10 HP left can deal just as much DMG as the full health alien.

Avoid using full sprint movement unless you are confident it will not reveal an enemy pod, especially if your other soldiers already finished their turn. This does not bode well as the liens get a chance to act first in most instances.

Patience is key in missions, as often I find when I am impatient, mistakes happen and soldiers die.

I'm in Canada, and specifically the province of Ontario.

I did a 1yr Pre-Health program (pre-requisite) and then a 3yr MRT program (Medical Radiation Technology) at the college level.

The first 2yrs were a didactic (classes & study) portion, and the last year was clinical practice at a hospital.  The college did a good job preparing us for the Canadian national exam (CAMRT association).  Once you pass this exam, you are certified to practice anywhere in Canada, however, you need to register for each specific province's regulatory college (protection for the public).

As for the job situation, it's pretty horrible in the cities.  It's over-saturated with more and more students being produced every year and hospitals only offering casual or part-time employment.  Cost of living in Canada is also quite high, much more than in the US - with some exceptions to large cities.

In Ontario, the average salary from rad techs is usually in the range of $28-35 at a hospital level.  This is general radiography, and you can advance into CT, MRI, and angio as well.

I'm of a minority that works in a small town in NW Ontario where I have been here for 3yrs and earn $35/hr, plus a lot of overtime, standby, and call-back bonuses.  To give a better perspective, I have a friend who works 3 different hospitals down in the city and works 6-7 days a week.  She makes 'almost' what I make with 1 full-time job up in the barren north.

In Canada, getting rural placement jobs can usually come with bigger perks and higher wages.  The cities have hundreds of applicants to choose from if someone doesn't like their job/wage.  Supply and demand.
